Why the open social web matters now

为什么开放社交网络现在很重要

The needs are real – and you have so much power.

需求是真实的 —— 而且你拥有如此大的权力。

Ben Werdmuller 本・韦德穆勒

14 Oct 2025 2025 年 10 月 14 日 — 17 min read 17 分钟阅读

I was privileged to deliver the opening keynote at this month's FediForum, a conference for people building and supporting the open social web. My talk touched on what's happening now, drew on my experiences building Elgg and Known and investing at Matter Ventures, and gave participants three important questions to ask themselves as they build platforms and serve communities.

我有幸在本月的联邦论坛 (FediForum) 上发表了开幕主题演讲，这是一个旨在帮助人们构建和支持开放社交网络的会议。我的演讲触及了当前正在发生的事情，借鉴了我在建立 Elgg 和 Known 以及投资 Matter Ventures 方面的经验，并给与会者提出了三个重要问题，让他们在构建平台和服务社区时自问。

Here's the talk in its entirety, courtesy of FediForum. The transcript follows below.

以下是完整的演讲内容，由联邦论坛提供。文字记录如下。

Introduction

引言

If we haven’t met, my name’s Ben Werdmuller. I’m based just outside of Philadelphia.

如果我们还没有见过面，我叫本・沃德穆勒。我的总部就在费城郊外。

Today, I’m the Senior Director of Technology at ProPublica, a non-profit newsroom here in the US that investigates abuses of power and betrayals of the public trust by government, business, and other institutions. If you remember the Clarence Thomas corruption scandal, Project 2025 co-author Russell Vought’s private remarks about how he was going to go after the left, or Peter Thiel’s tax-free investment scheme, that was our reporting.

今天，我是 ProPublica 的高级技术总监。ProPublica 是一家非营利性新闻编辑部，专门调查政府、企业和其他机构滥用权力和背叛公众信任的行为。如果你还记得克拉伦斯・托马斯腐败丑闻、2025 项目联合作者拉塞尔・沃特关于如何追随左派的私人言论，以及彼得・蒂尔的免税投资计划，那就是我们的报道。

I’m not a journalist but I’m very proud to support the people doing this journalistic work.

我不是记者，但我很自豪能支持从事这项新闻工作的人们。

But I actually started my career by building open source social networking platforms. I built a platform that allowed communities to self-host on their terms, using exactly the features that would support their needs. Elgg started in higher education, but it was used by NGOs like Greenpeace and Oxfam to train aid workers, it was used by the anti-austerity movement in Spain to help them organize, and Fortune 500 companies and at least one government used it as their primary intranet.

但实际上，我的职业生涯是从建立开源社交网络平台开始的。我建立了一个平台，允许社区按照自己的条件自我主导，使用的功能恰好能支持他们的需求。Elgg 最初从事高等教育，但它被绿色和平组织和乐施会等非政府组织用来培训援助工作者，被西班牙的反紧缩运动用来帮助他们组织，还被《财富》500 强公司和至少一个政府用作他们的主要内网。

We always wanted Elgg to federate. That was the plan from day one. It was an obvious need. There was no ActivityPub yet. We picked up on whatever tech we could — OpenID, Friend of a Friend — but ended up trying to cobble our own standard together. It wasn’t ActivityPub, and it didn’t work out quite as we’d hoped, but it began to touch on some of those underlying ideas.

我们一直希望埃尔格能联合起来。这是我们从第一天起就制定的计划。这是一个显而易见的需求。当时还没有 ActivityPub。我们尝试了所有可能的技术 ——OpenID、朋友的朋友 —— 但最终还是试图拼凑出我们自己的标准。这不是 ActivityPub, 效果也没有像我们希望的那样好，但它开始触及一些潜在的想法。

I built Known as a way for anyone to build feeds containing content of any type. It was mostly used by indie web bloggers, and it supported indie web standards for decentralized conversations, but it could support any number of users, and a feed could be published to by webhook and micropub, meaning theoretically any automatic system could post there.

我开发了 Known 作为一种方式，让任何人都可以创建包含任何类型内容的 feed。它主要被独立网络博主使用，并且支持独立网络标准的去中心化对话，但它可以支持任意数量的用户，feed 可以通过 webhook 和 micropub 发布，理论上意味着任何自动系统都可以在那里发布。

I led west coast investments for something called Matter, which supported early-stage mission-driven startups.

我领导了西海岸对一个叫 Matter 的公司的投资，该公司支持早期阶段的任务驱动型初创公司。

These were all ventures with the potential to create a more informed, inclusive, and empathetic society. That was our hypothesis. They had diverse teams and missions that weren’t a million miles away from the missions of people in this room.

这些都是有潜力创造一个更加知情、包容和富有同理心的社会的冒险。这是我们的假设。他们拥有多样化的团队和任务，这些任务与在座各位的任务相去不远。

And then I took a hard left turn and moved into leading technology for newsrooms, because I felt like that was the best way to be useful in this era. 

然后我来了个大转弯，转向了新闻编辑部的先进技术，因为我觉得这是在这个时代发挥作用的最好方式。

The 19th reports at the intersection of gender, politics, and policy - a much-needed inclusive newsroom in a world where much of our news is produced by white men in New York City. And I’ve already introduced you to ProPublica.

第 19 期报道位于性别、政治和政策的交汇处 —— 在一个大部分新闻都由纽约白人男性制作的世界里，这是一个亟需的包容性新闻编辑部。我已经向你介绍过 ProPublica。

So I’ve been involved in building platforms, supporting people who are building platforms, and leading technology in the kinds of organizations that we hope will be platform users. I’ve been on all sides of the table.

所以我一直参与平台建设，支持正在建设平台的人，并在我们希望成为平台用户的组织中引领技术发展。我已经涉足了各个领域。

And now, maybe ironically, while I’m not building or supporting platforms, open social networking is finally taking off. My timing has always been terrible, but I’m thrilled to be back in this conversation.

现在，也许有些讽刺的是，虽然我没有建立或支持平台，但开放式社交网络终于开始蓬勃发展。我的时机一直很糟糕，但很高兴能再次参与这场对话。

Why should anyone care?

为什么有人应该在乎呢？

I’d like to open FediForum with this provocation:

我想以这种挑衅的方式开启联邦论坛：

Why does this matter? Why should anyone care about decentralized or federated networks?

为什么这很重要？为什么有人应该关心去中心化或联邦化的网络？

Let’s start by examining the moment we’re in.

让我们从审视我们所处的时刻开始。

Here in the US, our government is becoming increasingly authoritarian. 

在美国，我们的政府正在变得越来越专制。

Immigrants are being ripped off the streets by masked officers without due process and often shipped to places like El Salvador or South Sudan. Just last week, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth told a roomful of American generals that he wanted them to fight “the enemy within” in the United States, echoing a phrase used in Nazi Germany.

移民正被蒙面军官从街上强行带走，没有经过正当程序，经常被运送到萨尔瓦多或南苏丹等地。就在上周，国防部长皮特・赫格塞特对一屋子的美国将军说，他希望他们在美国与 “内部敌人” 作战，这呼应了纳粹德国时期的一句话。

In Gaza, a UN commission found that there is indeed an ongoing genocide in progress. Many tens of thousands of people have been killed. Some of them were allegedly identified by a targeting AI through metadata from their WhatsApp chats.

在加沙，一个联合国委员会发现，一场正在进行的种族灭绝行动确实正在进行。数万人已经丧生。据称，其中一些人是由一个针对性的人工智能通过 WhatsApp 聊天中的元数据识别出来的。

Here in the US, students and journalists who have described it as a genocide have been detained or deported. Even liking a post on Instagram has been considered an actionable signal that you support terrorism by aligning yourself with Hamas.

在美国，那些将其描述为种族灭绝的学生和记者已经被拘留或驱逐出境。即使是在 Instagram 上点赞，也被认为是一个可行的信号，表明你通过与哈马斯结盟来支持恐怖主义。

And on some US-run social networks, people from Palestine who have been asking for help have been systematically removed.

在一些由美国运营的社交网络上，一直在寻求帮助的巴勒斯坦人已被系统性地删除。

National security policy now describes the following amongst signals that you might be a terrorist: 

国家安全政策现在在表明你可能是恐怖分子的信号中描述了以下内容：

“anti-Americanism, anti-capitalism, and anti-Christianity; support for the overthrow of the United States Government; extremism on migration, race, and gender; and hostility towards those who hold traditional American views on family, religion, and morality”.  “反美主义、反资本主义和反基督教；支持推翻美国政府；对移民、种族和性别的极端主义；以及对那些对家庭、宗教和道德持传统美国观点的人的敌意。”

People from communities that were already vulnerable - trans people among them - have been explicitly targeted, just as they were in 1930s Germany.

来自已经脆弱社区的人们 —— 其中包括跨性别者 —— 被明确地针对，就像他们在 20 世纪 30 年代的德国一样。

And speaking of trans people, they’re reportedly about to be classified as a nihilistic violent extremist threat group.

说到跨性别者，据报道他们即将被归类为虚无主义暴力极端主义威胁群体。

Categorizing these communities this way is a pretext to surveillance.

以这种方式对这些社区进行分类是监视的借口。

The CLOUD Act, passed in 2018, compels US-based online services (including US subsidiaries of foreign organizations) to share data with the US government regardless of where in the world that data is stored, and regardless of local regulations like GDPR. In the event of a criminal subpoena, including for suspected terrorist activity, you may never know your data was supplied.

2018 年通过的 CLOUD 法案强制美国在线服务 (包括外国组织的美国子公司) 与美国政府共享数据，无论数据存储在世界何处，也无论 GDPR 等地方法规如何。如果收到犯罪传票，包括涉嫌恐怖活动，你可能永远不会知道你的数据已被提供。

That was always creepy, but in a world where you may be profiled as a potential terrorist for having left-of-center opinions, or for being a member of a vulnerable group like the trans community, that really matters.

这一直让人感到毛骨悚然，但在这个世界上，你可能会因为持有偏左观点而被描绘成潜在的恐怖分子，或者因为是像跨性别群体这样脆弱群体的成员而被描绘成恐怖分子，这真的很重要。

The capitulation of social media

社交媒体的投降

The first step towards doing something about these events and threats to democracy is to know about them. How do we learn about them?

对这些事件和对民主政体的威胁采取行动的第一步是了解它们。我们如何了解它们？

In most western countries, social media and video networks are now our main source of news and the way we receive updates from our friends. A handful of companies own how we learn about the world, giving them the ability to shape our collective worldviews, influence movements, and prioritize their own interests. 

在大多数西方国家，社交媒体和视频网络如今是我们主要的新闻来源，也是我们从朋友那里获取最新消息的方式。少数公司拥有我们了解世界的方式，这使它们能够塑造我们的集体世界观，影响运动，并优先考虑自身利益。

They have never been great actors — Amnesty International accused Meta of platforming a genocide in Myanmar in 2017 — but their influence and power has never been greater than it is today.

他们从来都不是伟大的演员 ——2017 年，国际特赦组织指控 Meta 在缅甸策划了一场种族灭绝 —— 但他们的影响力和权力从未像今天这样大。

And every major commercial social network is complicit. They’re collaborators. 

每一个主要的商业社交网络都是共犯。他们是合作者。

We all know about Twitter acquirer Elon Musk, who bent the platform to fit his political worldview. But he’s not alone.

我们都知道 Twitter 收购者埃隆・马斯克，他扭曲了平台以适应自己的政治世界观。但他并不孤单。

Here’s Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, owner of LinkedIn, who contributed a million dollars to Trump’s inauguration fund.

这是微软首席执行官萨蒂亚・纳德拉，LinkedIn 的所有者，他向特朗普的就职基金捐赠了 100 万美元。

Here’s Mark Zuckerberg, who owns Threads, Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, who said that he feels optimistic about the new administration’s agenda.

这是马克・扎克伯格，他拥有 Threads、Facebook、Instagram 和 WhatsApp, 他表示对新政府的议程感到乐观。

And here’s Larry Ellison, who will control TikTok in the US, who was a major investor in Trump, and who one advisor called, in a WIRED interview, the shadow President of the United States.

这位是拉里・埃里森，他将控制 TikTok 在美国的业务。埃里森曾是特朗普的主要投资者，在接受《连线》杂志采访时，一位顾问称他为 “影子总统”。

Social media is very quickly becoming aligned with a state that in itself is becoming increasingly authoritarian.

社交媒体正在迅速与一个本身正在变得越来越专制的国家结盟。

The decline of journalism

新闻业的衰落

Journalism and the media is a way we’ve traditionally learned about the world. And a free press is usually a check on power. Multiple studies have found that communities with an active newsroom have less political corruption - or, rather, that communities without an active newsroom had more corruption.

新闻和媒体是我们传统上了解世界的方式。而新闻自由通常是对权力的检验。多项研究发现，有活跃新闻编辑部的社区政治腐败较少 —— 或者更确切地说，没有活跃新闻编辑部的社区腐败更多。

But the news industry failed to adapt to the more personal nature of the web, and has been in slow decline for many years.

但新闻业未能适应网络更加个人化的特性，多年来一直在缓慢衰落。

Compounding this, business decisions by companies like Google have led to fewer clickthroughs to news sites from search engines as well as from traditional social networks. They display AI summaries and show you answer boxes instead of prominently linking to the sources themselves.

更糟糕的是，像谷歌这样的公司的商业决策导致了来自搜索引擎和传统社交网络的新闻网站点击量减少。它们显示人工智能摘要，让你回答方框内容，而不是突出显示与信息来源本身的链接。

Fewer people clicking through translates to fewer pageviews, fewer subscribers, and fewer donors. Engagement and revenue are both declining. Public service journalism is withering just when we need it most.

点击量减少意味着页面浏览量减少，订阅者减少，捐赠者也减少。参与度和收入都在下降。公共服务新闻业正在我们最需要的时候凋零。

And now public media has been defunded by the government, driving the final nail into the coffin for many outlets. Hundreds of them have closed or are predicted to close soon.

现在，公共媒体已经被政府撤资，为许多媒体机构敲定了最后一根钉子。数百家媒体已经关闭，或者预计很快就会关闭。

Between the capitulation of social media and the slow decay of journalism, the result is less sunlight, more corruption, and more freedom for authoritarianism to spread and thrive.

在社交媒体投降和新闻业缓慢衰落之间，结果是阳光减少，腐败加剧，威权主义有更多自由传播和繁荣。

The problem is global

问题是全球性的

I’m speaking from the US context, but these aren’t US only problems. For one thing, America’s influence extends worldwide, both through agreements and through overarching legislation like the CLOUD Act. 

我是从美国的角度来说的，但这些不仅仅是美国的问题。首先，美国的影响力遍布全球，既通过协议，也通过像《云法案》这样的总体立法。

For another, there are parallel movements elsewhere. Over in Britain, a nationalist movement that started with Brexit is taking hold, while public journalistic institutions like the BBC are under threat. The Online Safety Act requires identity verification that can put people in vulnerable communities at risk, and the government seemingly continually asks for backdoors in privacy software. Similar patterns are emerging over much of Europe. Japan just elected a far right prime minister.

另一方面，其他地方也出现了类似的运动。在英国，一场始于英国脱欧的民族主义运动正在兴起，而英国广播公司等公共新闻机构正面临威胁。《在线安全法》要求进行身份验证，这可能使脆弱社区中的人们处于危险之中，而政府似乎不断要求在隐私软件中设置后门。类似的模式正在欧洲大部分地区出现。日本刚刚选出了一位极右翼的首相。

There’s a lot going on everywhere. It can be overwhelming. 

到处都在发生着很多事情。这可能会让人感到不知所措。

And whether you like it or not, sitting in this virtual room, you’re the counterculture. All of you are building platforms, communities, and relationships, with the potential to create an alternative to this centralization of power and influence.

无论你是否喜欢，坐在这个虚拟房间里，你就是反主流文化。你们所有人都在建立平台、社区和关系，有潜力创造一种替代这种权力和影响力集中的方式。

Social media and social networking

社交媒体和社交网络

We talk a lot about social media these days, but I want to register two definitions with you. Social media is the town square: a global commons where we can all learn from each other and build audiences at scale. Social networking, on the other hand, is a way to support communities of any kind using technology. These two things can interact and intersect, but they are not the same. 

最近我们经常谈论社交媒体，但我想向你们记录两个定义。社交媒体是城镇广场：一个全球性的公共场所，我们可以在那里相互学习，并大规模地建立受众群体。另一方面，社交网络是一种利用技术支持任何类型社区的方式。这两者可以相互作用和交叉，但它们并不相同。

Because of its emphasis on scale, I think social media is more predisposed to centralization, and because of its emphasis on relationships and communities, social networking is more predisposed to decentralization.

由于强调规模，我认为社交媒体更倾向于地方分权；而由于强调关系和社区，社交网络更倾向于地方分权。

Let's make this more concrete. Imagine I'm part of a rapid response network protecting immigrants from deportation without due process.

让我们把这个想法说得更具体一些。想象一下，我是一个快速反应网络的一员，这个网络保护移民免受未经正当程序的驱逐。

I have a core community. We trust each other completely. We coordinate the sensitive stuff in our private space: who has access to various resources, which volunteers are trained legal observers, how we move money to families when someone gets detained.

我有一个核心社区。我们完全信任彼此。我们在私人空间里协调敏感事务：谁能获得各种资源，哪些志愿者是受过培训的法律观察员，以及当有人被拘留时，我们如何向家属转移资金。

This inner circle needs to be absolutely secure. These conversations could get people deported if they fall into the wrong hands.

这个核心圈子必须绝对安全。如果这些对话落入错误的人手中，可能会导致人们被驱逐出境。

But our community can't cover a whole city. So we connect with other groups we trust: other mutual aid networks, immigrant rights organizations, faith communities that have offered sanctuary.

但我们的社区无法覆盖整个城市。所以我们联系了其他我们信任的团体：其他互助网络、移民权利组织、提供庇护的信仰社区。

These groups have their own secure spaces, their own trusted circles. But we need to coordinate with them. When ICE shows up to detain someone, we might need bodies there within 20 minutes: witnesses with cameras, legal observers, community members who can slow the process down and ensure due process is followed.

这些群体有自己的安全空间，自己的信任圈子。但我们需要与他们协调。当 ICE 出现逮捕某人时，我们可能需要在 20 分钟内派人到现场：带摄像头的证人、法律观察员、社区成员，他们可以减缓进程并确保正当程序得到遵守。

We're building an archipelago of trusted communities, each with their own secure space, but able to communicate across those boundaries.

我们正在建立一个由可信社区组成的群岛，每个社区都有自己的安全空间，但能够跨越这些界限进行沟通。

Together, across this archipelago, we can have private, end-to-end encrypted conversations about who's available for rapid response, where ICE was spotted this morning, which families need emergency funds.

我们可以一起，在这个群岛上进行私密的、端到端的加密对话，讨论谁可以提供快速反应，今天早上在哪里发现了 ICE, 哪些家庭需要紧急资金。

This encryption is vital. Without it, the web hosts that power our communities can be subpoenaed without our knowledge, and our conversations can be handed over to the government, putting everyone we're trying to help at risk.

这种加密至关重要。没有它，为我们社区提供动力的网络主机可能会在我们不知情的情况下被传唤，我们的对话可能会被移交给政府，将我们试图帮助的每个人置于危险之中。

So at this level, everything must be encrypted. The inner circles and the archipelago both need to be surveillance-proof.

所以在这个层面上，一切都必须加密。内圈和群岛都需要防止监控。

Federation makes us stronger. If one community is compromised for any reason and is taken offline, the others remain online. Just like the web itself.

联邦让我们变得更强大。如果一个社区因任何原因受到攻击并被下线，其他社区仍然会保持在线。就像网络本身一样。

And when we're ready, then we step into the public fediverse.

当我们准备好时，我们就会进入公共联邦世界。

We announce the action. We share the video. We name the officials responsible. We rally public support. Everyone has access to this: it's the town square, the place where we build power at scale.

我们宣布行动。我们分享视频。我们提名负责官员。我们团结公众支持。每个人都能接触到这个：这是城镇广场，是我们大规模建立权力的地方。

But we only got here safely because we could organize privately first.

但我们之所以能安全到达这里，只是因为我们可以先私下组织起来。

That's the distinction: networking builds trust and enables coordination within and across communities. Media scales that message to everyone.

这就是区别所在：网络能够建立信任，并使社区内部和跨社区的协调成为可能。媒体则将这一信息传递给每个人。

And the fediverse can do both. And it can do it without centralization, without being subject to any one company’s business decisions, and, if we add encryption, with freedom from surveillance. For vulnerable groups in particular, that provides a refuge, a place to build relationships and community, and, perhaps most crucially, a place to organize.

联邦快递可以做到这两点。它可以做到这一点，而不需要中央集权，不受任何一家公司商业决策的约束，如果我们再加上加密，还可以免受监视。特别是对于弱势群体来说，这提供了一个庇护所，一个建立关系和社区的场所，而且，也许最关键的是，一个组织的场所。

But these two modes - social media and social networking - are different modes with different use cases and different technical requirements.

但这两种模式 —— 社交媒体和社交网络 —— 是不同的模式，具有不同的使用案例和不同的技术要求。

In my example, each group hosts its own communications and controls its own data. They federate to form an archipelago with other trusted groups. At both of these levels, communications are end-to-end encrypted because they have to be. These conversations can’t happen safely without it being physically impossible for adverse actors, including the government, to obtain access to them without the active participation of the community itself. 

在我的例子中，每个群体都承载着自己的通信并控制着自己的数据。他们联合起来，与其他可信群体形成一个群岛。在这两个层面上，通信都是端到端加密的，因为它们必须如此。如果没有社区本身的积极参与，这些对话就无法安全地进行，因为对于敌对行为体 (包括政府) 来说，要获得访问权限在物理上是不可能的。

The fediverse is not inherently safer because it’s federated: an open, permissionless protocol can be exploited just as easily to surveil as it can to build.

Fediverse 并不因为是联邦的就天生更安全：一个开放的、未经许可的协议可以被利用来监控，就像它可以被建立一样容易。

But then, at the public level, those same groups can broadcast to the open fediverse when they need to.

但是，在公共层面上，这些同样的群体可以在需要时向开放的联邦协议广播。

The spec for MLS over ActivityPub covers these activities, and using it within a limited archipelago limits potential exposure to a set of trusted communities. Most fediverse platforms don't currently support this archipelago model. But the building blocks exist.

ActivityPub 上的 MLS 规范涵盖了这些活动，并且在有限的群岛范围内使用它限制了潜在接触一组可信社区的可能性。目前，大多数联邦平台都不支持这种群岛模式。但是，这些基本要素确实存在。

Start small

从小处着手

Of course, this isn’t limited to immigration protests or even activism. This model of small, trusted communities that intersect with the public sphere is already at the heart of the open social web. With the right tooling, it has applicability for journalism, for mutual aid, for co-operative culture, for collaborative marketplaces, and for every aspect of public life. The open social web is, I believe, and I know I’m preaching to the choir, the future of social and the future of the web.

当然，这不仅限于移民抗议甚至行动主义。这种由小型、可信赖的社区组成、与公共领域相互交织的模式，已经成为开放社交网络的核心。如果使用正确的工具，它适用于新闻、互助、合作文化、合作市场以及公共生活的各个方面。我相信，开放社交网络是，而且我知道我是在向合唱团宣讲社会和网络的未来。

So you might reasonably disagree with me about the threats, the needs, and this particular manifestation of a solution.

因此，你可能会合理地不同意我关于威胁、需求以及这种特定解决方案表现形式的观点。

But my point is not necessarily to advocate for this particular model. It’s when we’re building something new, we need to start somewhere small and specific. 

但我的观点并不一定是倡导这种特定的模式。当我们在构建新事物时，我们需要从一个小而具体的地方开始。

We need to start by supporting a specific community’s burning needs really well and grow outwards from there.

我们需要从很好地支持特定社区的迫切需求开始，然后从那里向外扩展。

Let's talk about TXTmob.

让我们来谈谈 TXTmob。

TXTmob was an SMS messaging service originally built by the Institute for Applied Autonomy for protesting political conventions in 2004, towards the beginning of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. Activists used it to coordinate actions, report on police movements, and share their whereabouts. A user would send their status update via SMS, and other members of the group would receive it. They refined it based on this very specific use case.

TXTmob 是一个短信服务平台，最初由应用自治研究所在 2004 年伊拉克和阿富汗战争爆发前夕为抗议政治集会而创建。活动分子使用它来协调行动、报告警方动向并分享他们的行踪。一位用户会通过短信发送他们的状态更新，该群体的其他成员会收到。他们根据这个非常具体的使用案例对其进行了改进。

After the Republican National Convention, there was a weekend session of hackers and activists. Two of the people there - Rabble and Blaine Cook - worked for a company called Odeo that was having trouble getting its social network for podcasting off the ground. They made some helpful suggestions that improved TXTmob, but they also did an internal presentation at Odeo about the tool and how it worked.

共和党全国代表大会之后，有一个黑客和活动家的周末会议。在场的两个人 ——Rabble 和 Blaine Cook—— 为一家名为 Odeo 的公司工作，该公司正在努力建立其用于播客的社交网络。他们提出了一些有益的建议，改进了 TXTmob, 但他们也在 Odeo 内部做了一次演示，介绍了这个工具及其工作原理。

A few days later, at an internal hackday, the team there prototyped a tool that worked very similarly. Eventually, they named it Twitter.

几天后，在一次内部开发日上，团队制作了一个工作方式非常相似的工具原型。最终，他们将其命名为 Twitter。

All of our microblogging tools have this lineage: short messages designed for a specific group of people and limited in length for a specific reason that was an outcome of that use case.

我们所有的微博工具都有这样的传承：针对特定群体设计的简短消息，由于特定原因而限制长度，这是那个用例的结果。

A specific use case led to a working prototype that led to a wider application. That pattern is repeated again and again.

一个特定的使用案例导致了一个工作原型，进而引发了更广泛的应用。这种模式一次又一次地重复。

Helping communities today

今天帮助社区

For the open social web to thrive, we need to go back to real communities with real-world use cases and solve their problems better than anything else. Not the needs of individuals within them, but of the interconnected communities themselves. We need to build social networks that deeply support their needs, and then social media that helps them thrive.

为了让开放社交网络蓬勃发展，我们需要回到具有真实世界用例的真实社区，比其他任何方法都更好地解决他们的问题。不是针对其中个人的需求，而是针对相互关联的社区本身。我们需要建立能够深刻支持他们需求的社交网络，然后是帮助他们蓬勃发展的社交媒体。

So if microblogging emerged from SMS updates for activists coordinating at the RNC in 2004, what should emerge from the needs of communities in 2025?

那么，如果 2004 年微博是从活动人士在 RNC 协调的短信更新中产生的，那么 2025 年应该从社区的需求中产生什么呢？

What does that look like in practice?

这在实践中是什么样子的？

I'd challenge anyone looking to start a new platform - or add features to an existing one - to ask three questions.

我会向任何想要启动一个新平台或为现有平台添加功能的人提出三个问题。

First: Who specifically do we want to help? 

首先：我们具体想要帮助谁？

Not "activists" or "journalists" in the abstract. Which organizers? Which newsrooms? Which communities? 

不是抽象意义上的 “活动家” 或 “记者”。是哪些组织者？哪些新闻编辑部？哪些社区？

Have you sat with them? Marched with them? Watched them work? Have you understood how they communicate and where their current tools fail them?

你和他们一起坐过吗？和他们一起游行过吗？看过他们工作吗？你理解他们如何沟通，以及他们当前的工具在哪些方面对他们不利吗？

Second: Why are we the right team to help them? 

其次：为什么我们是帮助他们的正确团队？

Is it lived experience in that community? Deep domain knowledge? A unique technical capability they need? Or are you building what you find intellectually interesting, rather than helping someone?

这是在那个社区中的亲身经历吗？深入的领域知识？他们需要的独特技术能力？还是你在构建你认为在智力上有趣的东西，而不是在帮助他人？

If your team isn't representative of the people you're trying to help, you might not be the right people yet.

如果你的团队不能代表你想要帮助的人，那么你可能还不是合适的人选。

Third: How can we address their needs better than anything else that exists today? 

第三，我们如何比当今任何其他方式都更好地满足他们的需求？

I don’t mean ideology. Open source or federation are not solutions in themselves. They’re characteristics of a solution.

我指的不是意识形态。开源或联盟本身并不是解决方案，而是解决方案的特征。

We need to be concretely meeting needs. Not what you think their needs are or what they should be, but what you’ve learned they are from getting to know them deeply.

我们需要具体地满足他们的需求。不是你认为他们的需求是什么或他们应该是什么，而是你通过深入了解他们所学到的东西。

What specific pain point are you solving that keeps people on WhatsApp despite the surveillance risk, or on X despite the white supremacy? 

你正在解决什么具体的痛点，让人们在面对监视风险时仍然使用 WhatsApp, 或者在面对白人至上主义时仍然使用 X?

What does open source or federation make possible that concretely makes their lives better today? Is it really better than Signal or email or whatever else they’re using?

开源或联盟是如何让他们的生活在今天变得更好的？它真的比 Signal、电子邮件或他们正在使用的其他任何东西都更好吗？

Concepts like "credible exit" are hypothetical. They matter in the long term, but they won't drive adoption today if the immediate experience isn't better. What’s making their lives better right now?

像 “可信退出” 这样的概念是假设性的。从长远来看，它们很重要，但如果当前的体验没有改善，它们就无法推动今天的采用。现在是什么让他们的生活变得更好？

It might be that you don’t have the answers today. 

也许你现在还没有答案。

Even then, there’s so much you can do. Maybe your role is to provide infrastructure, funding, technical support for communities building their own solutions - or just to promote the movement and spread the word. Maybe it’s about supporting and contributing to other projects in forums and communities like FediForum. Maybe you need to build your community or a team, building relationships and doing research until you do have the answers.

即便如此，你还有很多事情可以做。也许你的角色是为社区提供基础设施、资金和技术支持，帮助他们构建自己的解决方案 —— 或者仅仅是推动运动和传播信息。也许是支持和为论坛和社区 (如联邦论坛) 中的其他项目做出贡献。也许你需要建立你的社区或团队，建立关系并进行研究，直到你真正找到答案。

But I don’t think any social movement, any community, needs saviors riding in on a white horse.

但我不认为任何社会运动、任何社区需要骑着白马的救世主。

The world particularly does not need more tech teams swooping in to change the world from the basis of their own assumptions, even if they do believe in open source or federation. It needs more people willing to listen to the people who know, and to support people who are already on the ground.

这个世界尤其不需要更多的技术团队突然闯入，根据自己的假设来改变世界，即使他们确实相信开源或联邦制。它需要更多人愿意倾听那些了解情况的人，并支持那些已经在现场的人。

These questions work.

这些问题很有用

At Matter Ventures, I invested in and supported a portfolio of 75 startups, all of which were mission-driven, trying to make the world better in some key way. It taught me a lot about projects and how they succeed or fail.

在 Matter Ventures, 我投资并支持了 75 家初创公司的投资组合，这些公司都是以使命为导向的，试图以某种关键方式让世界变得更美好。这让我学到了很多关于项目的知识，以及它们如何成功或失败。

It turns out these questions for mission-driven open social web teams happen to be the same ones that most closely predicted whether one of those companies would live or die.

事实证明，这些关于使命驱动型开放社交网络团队的问题恰恰是最能准确预测其中一家公司生死存亡的问题。

If a team was trying to be the smartest people in the room and invent a solution without knowing, being of, and co-creating with the communities they were trying to help, they were not likely to succeed at what they were doing. The startups who were led by unwavering visionaries who thought they could invent something amazing because they were smart and clever and creative, with better values, were the ones that died fastest and hardest.

如果一个团队试图成为房间里最聪明的人，发明一个解决方案，却不了解、参与并与他们试图帮助的社区共同创造，那么他们不太可能在这项工作中取得成功。那些由坚定不移的远见者领导的初创公司，他们认为自己能够发明出令人惊叹的东西，因为他们聪明、聪明、富有创造力，拥有更好的价值观，恰恰是那些死得最快、最艰难的公司。

If, on the other hand, they did the work to understand their communities, make sure they were building something that really served them, made the effort to grow to be representative of them, and changed their focus when they learned that their communities needed something different to what they had in mind - those teams were much more likely to succeed.

另一方面，如果他们努力理解自己的社区，确保他们正在建设真正为自己服务的东西，努力成长为社区的代表，并在意识到社区需要与他们心目中不同的东西时改变焦点 —— 这些团队更有可能取得成功。

I realize most of this room probably doesn’t care about startups.

我意识到这个房间里的大多数人可能并不关心创业公司。

But again, not to belabor the point: the same questions that predicted whether mission-driven startups would succeed apply to everyone building on the open social web. Who are you building for? Why are you the right team? How does your solution concretely serve their real human needs better than anything else?

但是，再次强调，不要过分强调这一点：那些预测使命驱动型创业公司是否会成功的问题，同样适用于每个在开放社交网络上构建的人。你在为谁构建？为什么你是正确的团队？你的解决方案如何具体地比其他任何方法更好地满足他们的真实人类需求？

I’ve learned this first-hand.

这是我亲身体验到的。

I mentioned my two social networking projects, Elgg and Known. Elgg started with a concrete use case in higher education, then expanded to adjacent use cases in non-profits, and then to businesses and startups. It became a thriving business for years. Investors came to us asking to put money in. Several governments used it as their national intranets.

我提到了我的两个社交网络项目：Elgg 和 Known。Elgg 从高等教育的具体用例开始，然后扩展到相邻的非营利用例，最后扩展到企业和初创公司。它成为了一个多年来蓬勃发展的企业。投资者来找我们寻求投资。几个政府将其用作他们的国家内网。

Known was designed for the indie web, and had a community of people who were lovely people - they’re all my friends today - but they liked and supported us because of a certain set of shared values that we were in line with. It was ideological. There was no concrete real-world use case and Known had real trouble building traction.

Known 是为独立网站设计的，它有一个由可爱的人组成的社区 —— 他们现在都是我的朋友 —— 但他们喜欢我们并支持我们，因为我们有一套共同的价值观，这些价值观与我们一致。这是一个意识形态问题。它没有具体的现实世界用例，而 Known 在建立牵引力方面遇到了真正的困难。

The internal newsroom conversations I’ve had about the open social web have been disappointing to someone like me who cares about the space. They want to know why it’s better for their bottom line than the incumbent social networks that they already know how to measure and use. The answer can’t be ideological. There are real answers - people on the fediverse are more likely to engage in and donate to journalism, for example - but stories about how the fediverse is decentralized don’t land for them. It doesn’t speak to their needs.

对于像我这样关心开放社交网络空间的人来说，我在新闻编辑部内部进行的关于开放社交网络的讨论令人失望。他们想知道为什么它比他们已经知道如何衡量和使用的现有社交网络更有利于他们的利润。答案不可能是意识形态上的。确实有真实的答案 —— 例如，联邦快递员更有可能参与和捐款给新闻业 —— 但关于联邦快递如何去中心化的故事并不适合他们。这不符合他们的需求。

It turns out that if you solve a community’s needs deeply, you’re valuable to them. And these communities have intersecting communities, which you can get to know too, and be valuable to also. You’re more likely to reach sustainability, whatever your model is, because you’ll have communities that you’re serving deeply, who you’ve become valuable to, and who want to support you. That might be through donations or mutual aid or revenue or collaboration.

事实证明，如果你深入解决一个社区的需求，你对他们来说就是有价值的。这些社区有相互交织的社区，你也可以了解这些社区，并且对他们来说也是有价值的。无论你的模式如何，你都更有可能实现可持续发展，因为你会有一些你正在深入服务的社区，你对他们来说变得有价值，而且他们愿意支持你。这可能是通过捐赠、互助、收入或合作来实现的。

And we need the open social web to be sustainable. We need people to keep working on these problems. We need you to be able to work on this full-time without burning out.

我们需要开放社交网络的可持续性。我们需要人们继续致力于解决这些问题。我们需要你能够全职工作，而不会精疲力竭。

These aren't just good questions to ask: they're survival questions. Because the threats communities are facing aren't abstract and we need the open social web to exist.

这些不仅仅是值得问的好问题：它们是生存问题。因为社区面临的威胁并不抽象，我们需要开放的社交网络才能存在。

The threats are real

威胁是真实存在的

As I was writing this talk, an entire apartment building in Chicago was raided. Adults were separated into trucks based on race, regardless of their citizenship status. Children were zip tied to each other.

就在我写这篇演讲的时候，芝加哥的一整栋公寓楼遭到了突袭。成年人根据种族被分配到卡车上，不管他们的公民身份如何。孩子们则被用拉链绑在一起。

And we are at the foothills of this. Every week, it ratchets up. Every week, there’s something new. Every week, there’s a new restrictive social media policy or a news outlet disappears, removing our ability to accurately learn about what’s happening around us.

我们正处于这种状态的低谷。每周，这种状态都在恶化。每周，都有新事物出现。每周，都有新的限制性社交媒体政策或新闻媒体消失，使我们无法准确了解周围发生的事情。

And, look, I don’t mean to scare or pressure you. I really don’t. But you have so much power.

听着，我并不是想吓唬你或给你压力。我真的不是这个意思。但是你拥有如此强大的力量。

The threats are real. But so is the community in this room. You have the skills, the values, and now hopefully a framework to build what's needed.

威胁是真实的。但这个房间里的社区也是如此。你拥有技能、价值观，现在希望你有一个框架来构建所需的东西。

Everyone here has the potential to be building the future. You’re building platforms that provide an alternative to an authoritarian, extractive status quo, and every platform on the fediverse has the potential to help build a more informed and equal global society.

这里的每个人都有潜力建设未来。你们正在建设平台，为威权主义、榨取式现状提供替代方案，而联邦储备银行的每个平台都有潜力帮助建设一个更加信息化和平等的全球社会。

What I hope we'll all remember is that protocols and code are only valuable if they serve real communities with real needs. And today, there are communities facing real threats. 

我希望我们都能记住，协议和代码只有在服务于真实需求的真实社区时才有价值。而今天，有些社区正面临着真实的威胁。

The opportunity right now isn't to build a better Twitter or to provide a nice place for people who care about Linux to chat: it's to build infrastructure that vulnerable people can actually use to organize, to communicate safely, and to build community. But we can only do that if we're building with those communities from day one, not building for them based on our assumptions about what they need.

现在的机会不是建立一个更好的 Twitter, 也不是为那些关心 Linux 的人提供一个好的聊天场所：而是建立一个基础设施，让弱势群体能够真正用来组织、安全地沟通和建立社区。但我们只有从一开始就与这些社区一起建设，才能做到这一点，而不是基于我们对他们需求的假设来为他们建设。

Over the next two days, I hope you'll use those three questions as one of your lenses. Who is this really for? Are we the right people to build it? And does it concretely serve their real needs better than what exists today? Because the stakes are real, and there’s real scope to help.

在接下来的两天里，我希望你能将这三个问题作为你的视角之一。这究竟是为了谁？我们是建造它的正确人选吗？它是否比现有的更能切实地满足他们的真实需求？因为利害关系是真实存在的，而且有真正的帮助空间。

Thank you

谢谢你

Thanks for listening.

感谢您的倾听。

If you want to yell at me, I understand. Here’s where to find me.

如果你想对我大喊大叫，我理解。这是找我的地方。

  • Bluesky: 布鲁斯基：@werd.io
  • Web: 网站：werd.io
  • Email: 电子邮件：ben@werd.io
